6.0.s.en: 1. Daniel's position during the reign of Darius:

6.0.0.en: 1 It pleased Darius to set over the kingdom an hundred and twenty princes, which should be over the whole kingdom; 2 And over these three presidents; of whom Daniel was first: that the princes might give accounts unto them, and the king should have no damage. 3 Then this Daniel was preferred above the presidents and princes, because an excellent spirit was in him; and the king thought to set him over the whole realm.

6.0.1.en: Without doubt King Darius had heard of the prophet Daniel, and perhaps he saw him himself when Belshazzar was killed, and found him wearing the purple and the golden chain, so he inquired about his person. He learned that he was the one who had interpreted his dreams for Nebuchadnezzar, and for Belshazzar the writing that appeared on the wall before him. Darius honored him and trusted him, so he became the hand that God used to serve His captive people. But the enemy of good did not stand with folded hands, for the more God was glorified in Daniel, the more the enemy rose up to destroy him. God raised him in the eyes of the king to make him the next man after himself, while the enemy of good was preparing for him the pit of lions hungry to be rid of him and to destroy his work.

6.0.2.en: "It pleased Darius to set over the kingdom an hundred and twenty princes, which should be over the whole kingdom;

6.0.3.en: And over these three presidents; of whom Daniel was first: that the princes might give accounts unto them, and the king should have no damage.

6.0.4.en: Then this Daniel was preferred above the presidents and princes, because an excellent spirit was in him; and the king thought to set him over the whole realm" [1-3].

6.0.5.en: We have already spoken of Darius the Mede in chapter five. Some see that the period of the fall of Babylon is shrouded in some obscurity; perhaps Darius was until that time an unknown person to whom the kingship was entrusted by Cyrus. Although his identity is not yet established conclusively.

6.1.s.en: 2. The plan of the enemies against him:

6.1.0.en: 4 Then the presidents and princes sought to find occasion against Daniel concerning the kingdom; but they could find none occasion nor fault; forasmuch as he was faithful, neither was there any error or fault found in him. 5 Then said these men, We shall not find any occasion against this Daniel, except we find it against him concerning the law of his God. 6 Then these presidents and princes assembled together to the king, and said thus unto him, King Darius, live for ever. 7 All the presidents of the kingdom, the governors, and the princes, the counsellors, and the captains, have consulted together to establish a royal statute, and to make a firm decree, that whosoever shall ask a petition of any God or man for thirty days, save of thee, O king, he shall be cast into the den of lions. 8 Now, O king, establish the decree, and sign the writing, that it be not changed, according to the law of the Medes and Persians, which altereth not. 9 Wherefore king Darius signed the writing and the decree.

6.1.1.en: "Then the presidents and princes sought to find occasion against Daniel concerning the kingdom; but they could find none occasion nor fault; forasmuch as he was faithful, neither was there any error or fault found in him.

6.1.3.en: We shall not find any occasion against this Daniel, except we find it against him concerning the law of his God" [4-5].

6.1.4.en: * Blessed is the life that leads even the enemies so that they find in it no occasion for accusations except perhaps concerning the law of God.

6.1.5.en: St. Jerome "Then these presidents and princes assembled together to the king, and said thus unto him,

6.1.7.en: All the presidents of the kingdom, the governors, and the princes, the counsellors, and the captains, have consulted together to establish a royal statute, and to make a firm decree, that whosoever shall ask a petition of any God or man for thirty days, save of thee, O king, he shall be cast into the den of lions.

6.1.8.en: Now, O king, establish the decree, and sign the writing, that it be not changed, according to the law of the Medes and Persians, which altereth not.

6.1.9.en: Wherefore king Darius signed the writing and the decree" [4-9].

6.1.10.en: It is clear from the account that Darius was not king over the empire of the Medes alone, but over the joint empire of the Medes and Persians, as we saw in the previous chapter, since he was a partner in the rule with Cyrus.

6.1.11.en: The enemies devised their plan against Daniel out of envy, because of his greatness together with his godliness and his faithfulness to the king. They found no occasion against him, so they planned to be rid of him.

6.1.12.en: They persuaded the king that a decree like this would reveal the extent of the loyalty of the foreign captives to him in a new land.

6.2.0.en: 10 Now when Daniel knew that the writing was signed, he went into his house; and his windows being open in his chamber toward Jerusalem, he kneeled upon his knees three times a day, and prayed, and gave thanks before his God, as he did aforetime. 11 Then these men assembled, and found Daniel praying and making supplication before his God. 12 Then they came near, and spake before the king concerning the king's decree; Hast thou not signed a decree, that every man that shall ask a petition of any God or man within thirty days, save of thee, O king, shall be cast into the den of lions? The king answered and said, The thing is true, according to the law of the Medes and Persians, which altereth not. 13 Then answered they and said before the king, That Daniel, which is of the children of the captivity of Judah, regardeth not thee, O king, nor the decree that thou hast signed, but maketh his petition three times a day. 14 Then the king, when he heard these words, was sore displeased with himself, and set his heart on Daniel to deliver him: and he laboured till the going down of the sun to deliver him. 15 Then these men assembled unto the king, and said unto the king, Know, O king, that the law of the Medes and Persians is, That no decree nor statute which the king establisheth may be changed.

6.2.1.en: "Now when Daniel knew that the writing was signed, he went into his house; and his windows being open in his chamber toward Jerusalem, he kneeled upon his knees three times a day, and prayed, and gave thanks before his God, as he did aforetime" [10].

6.2.2.en: The enemies knew the time of Daniel's prayers, and it was easy to watch him from the open window. The Jews were accustomed to practice three daily prayers:

6.2.3.en: · In the morning, at the time of offering the morning sacrifice.

6.2.4.en: · At the ninth hour (3 p.m.), at the time of offering the evening sacrifice.

6.2.6.en: The prophet Daniel practiced his worship in the upper chamber, a sign of the soul's rising to the heights to meet God above all temporal things.

6.2.7.en: * Before all else our Lord celebrated the Passover in the upper chamber (Mt 14), and in the Acts of the Apostles the Holy Spirit came down on the hundred and twenty souls of believers while they were in the upper chamber (Acts 2). So also Daniel in this case, since he made light of the king's orders, and his confidence rested in God, did not practice his prayers in a hidden corner but in a high place, and opened his windows toward Jerusalem where he sees the peace of God.

6.2.8.en: Moreover he prayed according to God's commandment, and according to the word of Solomon, who urged the people to pray facing toward the temple.

6.2.9.en: * We must prostrate before God three times a day. According to the tradition of the Church, the three times are understood to be the third, sixth, and ninth hours. At the third hour the Holy Spirit came down on the Apostles (Acts 2:15). And at the sixth hour, when Peter wanted to eat, he went up to the upper chamber to pray (Acts 10). And at the ninth hour Peter and John were on their way to the temple (Acts 3).

6.2.10.en: St. Jerome "Then these men assembled, and found Daniel praying and making supplication before his God. Then they came near, and spake before the king concerning the king's decree;

6.2.11.en: Hast thou not signed a decree, that every man that shall ask a petition of any God or man within thirty days, save of thee, O king, shall be cast into the den of lions?

6.2.13.en: The thing is true, according to the law of the Medes and Persians, which altereth not.

6.2.14.en: Then answered they and said before the king,

6.2.15.en: That Daniel, which is of the children of the captivity of Judah, regardeth not thee, O king, nor the decree that thou hast signed, but maketh his petition three times a day.

6.2.16.en: Then the king, when he heard these words, was sore displeased with himself, and set his heart on Daniel to deliver him: and he laboured till the going down of the sun to deliver him.

6.2.17.en: Then these men assembled unto the king, and said unto the king,

6.3.0.en: Know, O king, that the law of the Medes and Persians is, That no decree nor statute which the king establisheth may be changed" [11-15].

6.3.1.en: St. Jerome says that just as the king understood the intention of these men, that they had devised the plan to ensnare Daniel, so they also understood the intention of the king, who abstained from food until sunset as a kind of pressure on them not to ask for Daniel's death, since it was not in his power to change the law he had issued, but they could have ignored what Daniel did and not complained against him. But they paid no heed to what the king did and insisted on applying the law to Daniel.

6.3.2.en: Daniel could have stopped praying for thirty days until the period of the decree ended, praying secretly in his house with the windows closed, and pretending that he was prostrating to the statue. But Daniel found his opportunity to declare his faith, so he opened the windows and challenged evil, not as a display of his strength, but as a witness to his faith. Daniel set certain times daily for prayer, and so was the Psalmist (Ps 55:16-17).

6.3.3.en: The enemies spoke against him with contempt and hatred: "This Daniel...", while the king stood as an advocate for him. But the enemies had made the plan firm, since the emperor had signed a law with no going back.

6.4.0.en: 16 Then the king commanded, and they brought Daniel, and cast him into the den of lions. Now the king spake and said unto Daniel, Thy God whom thou servest continually, he will deliver thee. 17 And a stone was brought, and laid upon the mouth of the den; and the king sealed it with his own signet, and with the signet of his lords; that the purpose might not be changed concerning Daniel. 18 Then the king went to his palace, and passed the night fasting: neither were concubines brought before him: and his sleep went from him. 19 Then the king arose very early in the morning, and went in haste unto the den of lions. 20 And when he came to the den, he cried with a lamentable voice unto Daniel: and the king spake and said to Daniel, O Daniel, servant of the living God, is thy God, whom thou servest continually, able to deliver thee from the lions? 21 Then said Daniel unto the king, O king, live for ever. 22 My God hath sent his angel, and hath shut the lions' mouths, that they have not hurt me: forasmuch as before him innocency was found in me; and also before thee, O king, have I done no hurt. 23 Then was the king exceeding glad for him, and commanded that they should take Daniel up out of the den. So Daniel was taken up out of the den, and no manner of hurt was found upon him, because he believed in his God. 24 And the king commanded, and they brought those men which had accused Daniel, and they cast them into the den of lions, them, their children, and their wives; and the lions had the mastery of them, and brake all their bones in pieces or ever they came at the bottom of the den.

6.4.1.en: "Then the king commanded, and they brought Daniel, and cast him into the den of lions.

6.4.2.en: Now the king spake and said unto Daniel,

6.4.3.en: Thy God whom thou servest continually, he will deliver thee" [16].

6.4.4.en: The king realized that the God of Daniel is the God of the impossible, for where all human arms fail to act, the power of God appears.

6.4.5.en: * The king left (the casting of Daniel) to the crowds, and did not dare to stop the plan of the enemies concerning the death of his friend, leaving it to the power of God to accomplish what he himself was unable to carry out.

6.4.6.en: He did not use the language of doubt as though saying: "If He is able to deliver you," but rather spoke with boldness and certainty: "Thy God whom thou servest, he will deliver thee." Surely he had heard of the three young men, who were of lower rank than Daniel himself, that they overcame the flame of Babylon. And he heard of the mysteries that were revealed to Daniel, so he looked on him with a lofty regard, and counted him in great honor, even though he was a captive.

6.5.0.en: St. Jerome "And a stone was brought, and laid upon the mouth of the den; and the king sealed it with his own signet, and with the signet of his lords; that the purpose might not be changed concerning Daniel" [17].

6.5.1.en: * He sealed the rock with his signet so that no one would open the den, so that the enemies of Daniel would not try to ensnare him. For he entrusted him into the hand of God, and although he was not troubled about the lions, he feared for him from men. He also sealed it with the seals of the nobles in order to avoid by every means any suspicion entering them.

6.6.0.en: St. Jerome "Then the king went to his palace, and passed the night fasting: neither were concubines brought before him: and his sleep went from him" [18].

6.6.1.en: * How sincere was the king's good intention, for he did not wish to touch food by night as by day, and gave no slumber to his eyelids. But since the prophet was in danger, he remained sympathizing with him in anxiety.

6.6.2.en: If the king who did not know God did this for the sake of another man whom he longed to save, how much more should we do, to appease the mercies of God with fasts and vigils on account of our sins?!

6.7.0.en: St. Jerome "Then the king arose very early in the morning, and went in haste unto the den of lions" [19].

6.7.1.en: The king hurried to the den in confidence in God, the God of Daniel, that He would save him.

6.7.2.en: "And when he came to the den, he cried with a lamentable voice unto Daniel:

6.7.3.en: Now the king spake and said unto Daniel,

6.8.0.en: O Daniel, servant of the living God, is thy God, whom thou servest continually, able to deliver thee from the lions?" [20].

6.8.1.en: * The king showed by his tears his inner affection, for he forgot his royal dignity, and his victory over the captives, and his lordship over his servant (Daniel)...

6.8.2.en: He called God the living God to distinguish Him from the gods of the Gentiles, who are like statues of the dead...

6.8.3.en: (This word of his) did not carry doubt about the power of God in whom he trusted... but he spoke it, not in doubt, but so that Daniel might appear unharmed, and so the king might find more justification for his anger against the nobles.

6.8.4.en: St. Jerome "Then said Daniel unto the king,

6.9.1.en: * Daniel honors the one who honored him, and asked that he live eternally.

6.10.0.en: St. Jerome "My God hath sent his angel, and hath shut the lions' mouths, that they have not hurt me: forasmuch as before him innocency was found in me; and also before thee, O king, have I done no hurt" [22].

6.10.1.en: * The one who prays and says: [Deliver not to the wild beasts the soul that confesseth thee] (cf. Ps 74:19), is heard, and suffers nothing from the asp and the serpents, because through Christ he is able to tread upon the lion and the dragon (Ps 91:13), and receives the glorious power which Jesus gives to tread on serpents and scorpions, and over all the power of the enemy (Lk 10:19), so nothing harms him from these things. Such a one must thank God more than Daniel, because he is delivered from beasts more terrifying and harmful.

6.10.2.en: * The mouths of invisible lions were stopped for the prophet Daniel so that all the more his soul might not be harmed by the visible lions.

6.10.3.en: Origen * Even these beasts can become harmless, unless it is a punishment falling on a sinner or a trial and approval of the perfection of the believer's virtues.

6.10.4.en: St. Augustine * Let every saint utter these words, and he will be snatched from the mouths of the invisible lions, and from the pit, because he trusts in his God.

6.10.5.en: St. Jerome "Then was the king exceeding glad for him, and commanded that they should take Daniel up out of the den.

6.10.6.en: So Daniel was taken up out of the den, and no manner of hurt was found upon him, because he believed in his God.

6.10.7.en: And the king commanded, and they brought those men which had accused Daniel, and they cast them into the den of lions, them, their children, and their wives;

6.11.0.en: and the lions had the mastery of them, and brake all their bones in pieces or ever they came at the bottom of the den" [23-24].

6.11.1.en: The story of the prophet Daniel here presents to us a living picture of the role of the individual in the life of the community. By his holy life Daniel succeeded, and he helped his three young companions, and also served his people in captivity, and served the kings and supported them, and served the Gentiles, for he presented to them clear prophecies about the Lord Christ. Thus, through his clinging to the Lord, his service while in captivity had no limits.

6.11.2.en: On the other hand, the corruption that came upon his envious enemies cost them their peace, and turned their energy to demolition instead of building up, and shattered the king's peace for a time, and drove them with their wives and children into the den to become prey for the hungry lions. So it is fitting for us not to make light of our lives: in every inner building up we support many and heaven rejoices over us, and with every deviation we pull down many with us and because of us a great tempest arises, as happened because of Jonah who fled from the presence of the Lord. The custom of an entire family falling under punishment was known in ancient societies, and it conflicts with what is written in (Deut 24:16; Jer 31:29 etc.; Ezek 18).

6.11.3.en: The king failed to rescue Daniel because the decree had already been signed and there was no going back, but God Himself saved him.

6.11.4.en: The king was in his palace exceedingly sorrowful, sleep fled from his eyes, while the wicked who devised the plan were in great joy. Perhaps they gathered to congratulate themselves on the success of their plan and their being rid of Daniel. Perhaps they were planning that night to nominate a man to take Daniel's place. As for Daniel, he returned to the first paradisal life where there is strong friendship between animals, even the predatory ones, and man. He played with these animals and caressed them for the first time in his life, and he experienced the pledge of heaven, for an angel came down and shut the lions' mouths. Daniel spent the happiest and most wonderful night of his entire life.

6.11.5.en: Had the king not cast the wicked into the den, it could have been said that the lions were not hungry, and therefore Daniel was not harmed. But he remained with them a whole night in peace and safety, while the lions were seized with a state of near madness when many were thrown into the den, so that they did not wait for them to reach the floor and crushed all their bones while they were being thrown in... This revealed the hand of God that saved the prophet Daniel with power, and removed the slightest doubt that could trouble anyone.

6.11.6.en: Daniel rested, not because he was delivered from bodily death, but because he enjoyed a new vision and a deeper awareness of God's love and care for him. As for the king, he did not rest because he felt he had lost the dearest faithful man to him, and realized that he had practiced injustice against one who was loyal to him. But he hoped in God, the God of Daniel, that He would save that faithful man.

6.11.7.en: We can say that the prophet Daniel praised God in the midst of the lions' den, saying with the Psalmist: "Thou shalt tread upon the lion and adder: the young lion and the dragon shalt thou trample under feet. Because he hath set his love upon me, therefore will I deliver him: I will set him on high, because he hath known my name. He shall call upon me, and I will answer him: I will be with him in trouble; I will deliver him. With long life will I satisfy him, and shew him my salvation" (Ps 91:13-16). As for the enemies of Daniel, the saying of the prophet Amos applies: "As if a man did flee from a lion, and a bear met him; or went into the house, and leaned his hand on the wall, and a serpent bit him. Shall not the day of the LORD be darkness, and not light? even very dark, and no brightness in it?" (Amos 5:19-20).

6.11.8.en: Since God saved Daniel, the king decided to punish the wicked and their families who had plotted against the righteous prophet Daniel.

6.12.0.en: 25 Then king Darius wrote unto all people, nations, and languages, that dwell in all the earth; Peace be multiplied unto you. 26 I make a decree, That in every dominion of my kingdom men tremble and fear before the God of Daniel: for he is the living God, and stedfast for ever, and his kingdom that which shall not be destroyed, and his dominion shall be even unto the end. 27 He delivereth and rescueth, and he worketh signs and wonders in heaven and in earth, who hath delivered Daniel from the power of the lions. 28 So this Daniel prospered in the reign of Darius, and in the reign of Cyrus the Persian.

6.12.1.en: "Then king Darius wrote unto all people, nations, and languages, that dwell in all the earth;

6.12.3.en: I make a decree, That in every dominion of my kingdom men tremble and fear before the God of Daniel: for he is the living God, and stedfast for ever, and his kingdom that which shall not be destroyed, and his dominion shall be even unto the end.

6.12.4.en: He delivereth and rescueth, and he worketh signs and wonders in heaven and in earth,

6.12.5.en: who hath delivered Daniel from the power of the lions" [25-27].

6.12.6.en: Darius' proclamation was stronger than the proclamation of Nebuchadnezzar (Dan 3:29), because it was positive, not negative. Darius was moved by what happened, and his depths were shaken before the miracle. He realized that the true living God, the God of Daniel, is the eternal One who does not die, who moves heaven and earth with power to save His believers. This does not mean that Darius became godly, for he did not remove from his palace or his kingdom the pagan worship, nor did he remove from his conduct what is unbecoming for believers. He glorified God for a time, but he remained in pagan abominations.

6.12.7.en: The king called God "the God of Daniel," just as God was previously attributed to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, but since he did not enjoy the experience of life with God, the king could not attribute God to himself. We need to enjoy God as our God, who longs to attribute Himself to us, as we attribute ourselves to Him, so that we say with the prophet Jeremiah: "The LORD is my portion, saith my soul" (Lam 3:24). And we hear the voice of the Lord saying: "He that overcometh shall inherit all things; and I will be his God, and he shall be my son" (Rev 21:7).

6.12.8.en: The king speaks of God as a Savior who delivered and delivers Daniel, but he did not come forward to enjoy the divine mercies himself, and to taste His fatherhood in his personal life.

6.12.9.en: He praised God as the maker of signs and wonders in heaven and on earth, for he knew all that happened with his fathers, and what was accomplished at the hands of the prophet Daniel, but he did not enjoy the signs in his depths. He did not surrender his body and soul, as earth and heaven, for God to move with His strong hand, and to declare His wonders in them!

6.12.10.en: Some have asked whether the den could hold 120 princes with their wives and children. The answer is that only a few of them were cast into the den, those who had complained against Daniel.

6.12.11.en: The accuracy of the story appears in that, according to Persian customs, the relatives of a man were punished for the guilt of his crime, and for this reason the wives and sons were also cast in.

6.13.0.en: "So this Daniel prospered in the reign of Darius, and in the reign of Cyrus the Persian" [28].

6.13.1.en: The chapter ends with the news of Daniel's prospering "in the reign of Darius, and in the reign of Cyrus the Persian." For since this was in the days of the kingdom of Persia and Media, Darius the Mede was the one entrusted with its affairs as a partner ruler with Cyrus the Persian, so the text does not mean two successive reigns, and recent archaeological discoveries have come to confirm this.

6.13.2.en: The prophet Daniel prospered in the days of the Chaldeans or the Babylonian kingdom, where he was taken captive to Babylon and was chosen as one of the wise men who stand before the king (Dan 1), and God gave him favor in the eyes of Nebuchadnezzar, for he interpreted dreams for him, but he was probably excluded through the envy of the magicians, the soothsayers, and the wise men. And in the last moments of the life of Belshazzar, the last king of Babylon, he was brought back to read what the hidden hand had written on the wall of the palace. And when Darius and Cyrus conquered Babylon they gave him special honor; Darius the Mede honored him in his old age until he died, and Cyrus the Persian, the son of Darius' sister, counted him among his great men who were near to him. Thus God turned Daniel's sorrows in captivity into consolations. He prospered in his daily life and in his words as in his work. He served his generation with power, and served the following generations of the Gentiles as well as the Jews through his prophecies that are recorded in the second part of the book.

6.13.3.en: Without doubt Daniel was sad, not because he was taken captive like many of the peoples whom Nebuchadnezzar subdued, but even more because he was deprived of the Promised Land, and of enjoying the holy city and the temple of the Lord. But God used him for a greater work among the peoples, and for a surpassing mission that continues through the generations. Thus God gave him prosperity according to the divine mind and not according to our human mind. He was deprived of the temple in Jerusalem, but he stood before the new temple of the Lord to open the doors of hope for the Gentiles to enjoy the divine holy things, so it was right for him to sing: "I had rather be a doorkeeper in the house of my God, than to dwell in the tents of wickedness" (Ps 84:10). For this reason the prophet Ezekiel counted him one of the three great men of old: "Noah, Daniel, and Job" (Ezek 14:14).

6.14.s.en: Turn love into a heaven for me!

6.14.0.en: * Wonderful is Your care, O Pantocrator!

6.14.1.en: You allow me, with Daniel, to be cast into the midst of the den, but You turn the den into a paradise!

6.14.2.en: You grant me to see Your angels, those who serve us for salvation, and who delight in working on behalf of Your Kingdom in us!

6.14.3.en: * Cast me into the den, but shut the mouths of the hungry lions so that they do not harm me.

6.14.4.en: * In my bewilderment I see as though everyone is against me.

6.14.5.en: But I find, even among the unbelievers, Darius the faithful king!

6.14.6.en: I am ashamed before him for his sincerity and his trust in You!

6.14.7.en: For Daniel's sake he did not eat until sunset, and his fast even lasted until dawn.

6.14.8.en: He refrained even from his human rights for the sake of his servant Daniel!

6.14.10.en: And at dawn he ran to the den!

6.14.11.en: * He called to Daniel with a lamentable voice, so that those around him might know that the God of Daniel is able to deliver completely!

6.14.13.en: Should I fast and weep for the salvation of my brethren, and even for the salvation of the whole world?!

6.14.14.en: Should I trust the God of Daniel who is able to deliver?

6.14.15.en: Should I not give my eyes sleep while there are souls in the den of invisible lions?!

6.14.16.en: Should I rise early to search for every soul?!
